title: Rails, Homesteads and Bison
objective: After this level you can explain how the transcontinental railroad and the Homestead Act opened the Plains, and how the bison were nearly wiped out.
summary: In 1869 two railroads met at Promontory Summit, and the Homestead Act drew settlers west. Railways, hide hunters and the army cut the bison from tens of millions to under 1,000.

cards.headline: Trains crossed the continent in 1869. By the 1890s the bison were nearly gone.
cards.body: The same years that tied the country together with iron almost wiped out the animal the Plains nations lived on. Here’s how rails, farms and hunters remade the Plains.

cards.headline: Two railroads race to meet
cards.body: In 1862 Congress passed the first Pacific Railroad Act. The Union Pacific built west from Nebraska, the Central Pacific built east from California, and the two lines met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869. By the end, Chinese immigrants made up about 90 percent of the Central Pacific’s workforce. The country’s new steel spine was built largely by immigrant hands.
cards.callout: The rails met at Promontory Summit, Utah, on May 10, 1869

cards.headline: Free land, with conditions
cards.body: In 1862 Lincoln also signed the Homestead Act. It offered 160 acres of public land for a filing fee, as long as you lived on it and farmed it. The people who tried to “prove up” came from all walks of life: immigrants, farmers without land of their own, single women and formerly enslaved people. A farm of your own, for the price of hard work and paperwork.

cards.headline: The Great Slaughter
cards.body: Bison once numbered an estimated 30 to 60 million. Railways, rifles and an international market for hides drove the “Great Slaughter,” from about 1820 to 1880. The US military also encouraged destroying the herds, as a way to control the Native nations who depended on them. By the 1890s, fewer than 1,000 bison were left. A whole way of life was losing its foundation.

mascot.line: It connects: Level 7’s horses made Plains peoples expert bison hunters. Lose the bison, and that whole way of life is under attack.

cards.headline: Rails, homesteads and bison: explained
learned: Two railroads met at Promontory Summit in 1869
Chinese immigrants built most of the Central Pacific
The Homestead Act offered 160 acres to settlers
Bison fell from tens of millions to under 1,000

questions.prompt: Match each railroad or law with its description.
questions.explanation: The Union Pacific built west from Nebraska and the Central Pacific built east from California. The Homestead Act offered 160 acres of public land to settlers who lived on it and farmed it.

questions.prompt: Why did the bison herds collapse so fast in the 1800s?

options.label: A long drought dried up the grasslands the herds needed
options.rationale: Mass killing for hides, not drought, destroyed the herds.

options.label: Homesteaders fenced the herds in and let them starve
options.rationale: The herds were shot for their hides, not starved.

options.label: Rails, rifles and a hide market drove mass killing, with army support
Plains peoples stopped hunting them, so the herds grew old and died out
options.rationale: Plains peoples depended on the bison.

questions.explanation: Railways, rifles and the hide trade drove the Great Slaughter, and the military encouraged it to control Native nations.

questions.prompt: Horses had made Plains peoples far better bison hunters. What happened to the bison by the 1890s?

options.label: They had spread east of the Mississippi
options.rationale: The herds collapsed rather than spreading.

options.label: They numbered about 30 to 60 million
options.rationale: That was the estimate before the slaughter.

options.label: They had been replaced by wild horses
options.rationale: Horses did not replace the bison.

questions.explanation: From an estimated 30 to 60 million, the bison fell to fewer than 1,000 by the 1890s.
